client: I've been really stressed since losing my job back in February. The job market seems so competitive now, and every time I try to update my resume, I just freeze up because I don't know how to make myself stand out. The worst part is watching my savings dwindle while I feel stuck in this cycle of anxiety and procrastination.
therapist: It sounds like this has been a really difficult and overwhelming time for you, especially with the added pressure of financial worries. When you think about updating your resume, what thoughts come up that make you feel stuck or unsure?

client:
I just freeze up when I think about my resume because it feels like no matter what I put down, it won't be good enough. I keep thinking about how I've been out of work for months now, and that gap makes me feel like employers will just toss my application right away. 

Even when I try to start, my mind goes blank and I end up closing my laptop because the whole process makes me feel so inadequate.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught in a cycle of self-doubt and frustration, which makes starting feel impossible right now. When you think about that gap in your resume, what evidence do you have that employers will see it negatively—and could there be other ways they might view it?

client:
I get what you're saying, but it's hard not to assume the worst. Every job posting seems to want someone with continuous experience, and I keep imagining hiring managers tossing my resume aside when they see that gap. Even if there might be other ways to look at it, I can't shake this feeling that I'm already at a disadvantage before I even apply. 

The logical part of me knows gaps happen, but the anxious part keeps coming up with worst-case scenarios about how I'll be judged. It makes me procrastinate on applications because why bother if they'll just reject me anyway?
therapist: It’s clear that the fear of rejection is really weighing on you, and it’s understandable to feel stuck when those worst-case scenarios feel so vivid. What would it look like to focus on small, manageable steps—like updating just one section of your resume—rather than trying to tackle it all at once?

client:
I know breaking it down should help, but even updating one section feels overwhelming right now. What if I do it wrong or it still isn't good enough? I keep imagining hiring managers laughing at my resume and that makes me freeze up. 

The small steps approach makes logical sense, but my brain keeps jumping to "what's the point if I'll just get rejected anyway?" It's frustrating because I know this thinking isn't helping me.
therapist: It sounds like the fear of judgment is so intense right now that even small steps feel risky, and that frustration with yourself is adding another layer of difficulty. What would happen if, just for a few minutes, you allowed yourself to write a "bad" first draft—no pressure, just getting thoughts on paper?

client:
I get what you're saying, but even the idea of writing a "bad" draft makes me anxious. What if I read it later and it confirms all my worst thoughts about myself? I already feel like such a mess inside, and seeing it on paper might just make that feeling worse. 

It's not that I don't want to try, but I can't shake this fear that putting my thoughts down will make them more real somehow. Like if I write "I'm worthless" even as an exercise, that means I'm admitting it's true.
therapist: It sounds like putting these thoughts on paper feels dangerously final—like they might cement your fears rather than help you work through them. What if we tried framing it differently: instead of writing your thoughts as truths, what if you wrote them down as "just thoughts" to observe, not facts to believe?

client: I get what you're saying about treating thoughts as just thoughts, but it's hard when they feel so real in the moment. When I'm anxious, these thoughts don't feel optional—they feel like warnings I have to pay attention to. Writing them down still makes me nervous because what if I can't stop obsessing over them afterward?
therapist: It makes sense that these thoughts feel urgent and important when anxiety takes over—like warnings you can't ignore. What do you think would happen if, just for now, we focused on observing these thoughts without trying to change or stop them? Could they lose some of their power that way?

client: I get what you’re saying, but it’s hard to just observe the thoughts without reacting. They feel so real, like if I don’t act on them, something bad will happen. It’s like my brain is screaming at me to pay attention, and ignoring it feels dangerous, you know? I’m not sure if observing them will make them lose power—it might just make me feel more overwhelmed.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real fear that stepping back from these thoughts might leave you unprotected, and that makes observing them feel risky right now. What if we tried something small—just noticing one thought today, without needing to change it, to see how that feels?

client: I get what you're saying, but it’s hard to just notice a thought without reacting to it. My mind always jumps to worst-case scenarios, and if I don’t try to stop those thoughts, I feel like I’m letting something bad happen. It’s like I have to keep control, or everything will fall apart. How can just noticing one thought even help with that?
therapist:
It makes complete sense that stepping back from those thoughts feels like losing control—like you're dropping your guard against the worst-case scenarios your mind creates. That fear of "everything falling apart" is so real in those moments. 

What if we tried this: instead of stopping the thought or fully believing it, could you just name it? Like, "Ah, there's the 'everything will fall apart' thought again." Not to change it, just to acknowledge it's there—like noticing a passing cloud. How does that idea sit with you?

client:
I get what you're saying about naming the thought, but it feels like that would just make me focus on it even more. When I notice anxious thoughts, they tend to grow louder instead of fading away. It's like poking at a bruise—the more attention I give it, the more it hurts. 

I also worry that if I start naming these thoughts, I'm just giving them permission to stick around instead of fighting them off like I usually do. Doesn't that make the anxiety worse in the long run?
therapist:
It sounds like naming the thoughts feels counterintuitive right now—almost like you'd be feeding the anxiety rather than easing it. That worry makes total sense, especially when these thoughts already feel so intrusive. 

What if we experimented with this just once today, not to change anything, but to see what happens when you gently notice a thought without fighting it—almost like testing a hypothesis? How does that sound to you?

client:
I get what you're saying about testing it as an experiment, but I'm worried that if I actually name the anxious thought out loud, it'll make it feel more real. Like giving it power over me. 

I've tried ignoring these thoughts before and that doesn't work either, but at least that way I don't feel like I'm inviting them in. Does that make sense?
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between two approaches—ignoring the thoughts or naming them—and both feel risky in their own way, leaving you stuck in this cycle. That frustration is completely understandable. 

What if we tried something in between: instead of ignoring or fully engaging, could you simply note, "Anxiety is here," without diving into the specifics of the thought? Just acknowledging its presence, not its content. How does that land for you?
